The classic PEC ground plane model can be off by 5 dB or more in predicting cavity RCS compared to measurements.
The IBC ground plane model approximates an infinite radar absorbing screen and better matches experimental setups.
Kirchhoff-type aperture integration is used to compute scattered far-fields from cavity apertures.
The finite element–infinite element (FE-IE) method is employed to solve the coupled interior-exterior scattering problem.
The physical optics modification to the PEC model accounts for the virtual PEC lid scattering contribution.
Verification examples include prismatic PEC cavities at 0.3 GHz and 10 GHz, and cylindrical PEC cavities at 9.13 GHz and 15.20 GHz.
The IBC model predictions agree well with mode matching and FE-BI numerical results from literature.
Measurements from Lee and Lee on a cylindrical PEC cavity validate the IBC model's accuracy.
The scattering contribution from the aperture lid is largest at normal incidence and decreases exponentially with angle.
The PEC model assumes perfect reflection from an infinite conducting plane, neglecting radar absorbing material effects.
Infinite elements enforce the Silver–Müller radiation condition in the exterior domain.
The domain decomposition approach partitions the computational domain into near-field, cavity, and far-field regions.
The electric current on the PEC plane is approximated as uniform for the superposition principle to hold.
The aperture diameter must be large relative to the wavelength for Kirchhoff approximations to be valid.
The IBC model provides an efficient half-space replacement for full-space cavity scattering problems.
The paper provides a convergence study showing discretization errors below 0.06 dB in RCS predictions.
The modified PEC GP model or the IBC model can be used interchangeably for electrically large apertures.
The paper explains why the classic PEC GP model fails for the 'simple jet engine' benchmark problem.
The scattered far-field is obtained by an exact integral formula involving the effective magnetic current on the aperture.
